pairs.evidence_text: Based on the assessment’s detailed measurement of math skills, it shows that each weekly hour of math instruction in a given topic increases student test scores in that topic by 4.3% of a SD.
These analyses unveil substantial differentials in instructional productivity among U.S. math teachers based on the teaching practices they implement in the classroom.

A first strand of the literature provides consistent evidence that teacher experience (Dinerstein et al., 2022; Papay & Kraft, 2015; Wiswall, 2013), subject-knowledge (Bau & Das, 2020; Bietenbeck et al., 2018; Hanushek et al., 2019; Metzler & Woessmann, 2012) and measures of teaching quality based on classroom observation from an external evaluator (Araujo et al., 2016; Blazar, 2015; Burgess et al., 2023; Kane et al., 2011) relate to higher levels of teacher value-added.

A first strand of the literature provides consistent evidence that teacher experience (Dinerstein et al., 2022; Papay & Kraft, 2015; Wiswall, 2013), subject-knowledge (Bau & Das, 2020; Bietenbeck et al., 2018; Hanushek et al., 2019; Metzler & Woessmann, 2012) and measures of teaching quality based on classroom observation from an external evaluator (Araujo et al., 2016; Blazar, 2015; Burgess et al., 2023; Kane et al., 2011) relate to higher levels of teacher value-added.

Several studies also demonstrate that programs based on teacher training, external evaluation or peer learning can increase teacher productivity (Angrist & Lavy, 2001; Briole & Maurin, 2024; Harris & Sass, 2011; Jackson & Bruegmann, 2009; Papay et al., 2020; Taylor & Tyler, 2012).

The fact that TIMSS tests both taught and untaught subtopics – randomly across students – and that teachers have no information about which ones will be assessed, creates a unique opportunity to implement falsification tests.
For example, due to sorting of students both across and within schools, students with higher academic ability could benefit from more instructional time.

I include a rich set of teacher- and class-level controls interacted with 𝐼𝑇𝑗𝑡 . These include teacher gender, educational level, years of experience, and academic background (math or math education).

To check the validity of this assumption, I conduct a falsification test in Section 3.1, showing that instructional time has no effect on student performance in subtopics that were not taught during the year.

The coefficient for COMPEX is 0.783, which corresponds to the log of odds ratio between students who have computer experience for five years or more and those who do not.
The coefficient for S_INTNET is 0.886, which corresponds to the log of odds ratio between students who have internet connection at home and those who do not.
The coefficient for S_SEX is 0.767, which corresponds to the log of odds ratio between the female group and male group.

The coefficient for ISCED is 0.399, which corresponds to the log of odds ratio between students whose parents’ level of education is undergraduate or above and students whose parents’ level of education is below undergraduate.
